entry: Branch of mathematical analysis that develops [[Calculus|calculus]] rigorously over the [[Real number|real numbers]] and [[Euclidean space|Euclidean spaces]]. It studies [[Limit (mathematics)|limits]], continuity, compactness, differentiation, integration, and series. Completeness, the property that every nonempty set bounded above has a least upper bound, underlies the convergence of bounded monotone sequences and the intermediate value theorem. Pointwise limits of continuous functions are not generally continuous, which is why real analysis distinguishes pointwise from uniform convergence. Advanced courses add measure theory, Lebesgue integration, and function spaces. Older books also call it the theory of functions of a real variable, in contrast to the theory of complex variables.

Property consisting of land and the buildings on it, together with its natural resources, such as crops, minerals, water, and wild animals. It differs from personal property, which is not permanently attached to land, such as vehicles, boats, furniture, and farm animals. Ownership may be private, public, or commercial, and use may be residential or commercial; an [[Apartment|apartment]] block owned by a business but intended for residential use is one example. In the [[United States]], corporations, individuals, nonprofit corporations, and other legal entities may hold real estate under each state's law. The [[Louisiana Purchase]] of 1803, in which the United States bought the Louisiana Territory from France for fifteen million dollars, was one of the largest early real estate deals. After the stock market crash of 1929, values depreciated 50% over the following four years. The National Association of Realtors was founded in Chicago in 1908.

[[Genre|Genre]] of television programming that documents purportedly unscripted real-life situations, often starring ordinary people rather than professional actors. It emerged as a distinct genre in the early 1990s with *The Real World*, and gained prominence in the early 2000s with *Survivor*, *Idol*, and *Big Brother*, all of which became global franchises. Shows often include "confessionals," short interviews in which cast members comment on events. Competition formats eliminate participants by judges, by viewers, or by the contestants themselves. Documentaries, news, sports, [[Talk show|talk shows]], and traditional [[Game show|game shows]] are generally not classified as reality television. Critics argue that artificial situations, coached behavior, staged scenes, and misleading editing mean the shows do not accurately reflect reality. Others object that they humiliate or exploit participants and glamorize vulgarity.

American [[Country music|country]] singer and actress, dubbed "The Queen of Country." She has placed more than 100 singles on the Billboard Hot Country Songs chart, 24 of them at number one. Raised in Oklahoma, she sang with her siblings in the Singing McEntires before signing with PolyGram/Mercury Records in 1975. Her 1984 album *My Kind of Country*, released on MCA Records, became her breakout. In 1991 a plane crash in [[San Diego]] killed eight of her band members, and her album *For My Broken Heart* followed. She starred in the sitcom *Reba*, which aired for six seasons, and played [[Annie Oakley]] in the Broadway musical *Annie Get Your Gun*.

Gothic novel by English author Daphne du Maurier, first published in 1938. An unnamed young woman marries the wealthy widower Maxim de Winter after meeting him in [[Monte Carlo]]. At Manderley, his estate in [[Cornwall]], she finds the household still haunted by the memory of his first wife, Rebecca. Its best-known character is the housekeeper Mrs. Danvers. The novel has never gone out of print and sold 2.8 million copies between 1938 and 1965. The 1940 film *Rebecca*, directed by [[Alfred Hitchcock]], won the Academy Award for Best Picture. A 2020 [[Netflix]] adaptation was directed by Ben Wheatley.

Turkish politician, president of [[Turkey]] since 2014. Coming from an Islamist background, he was elected mayor of [[Istanbul]] in 1994 and was banned from politics after a 1998 conviction for inciting religious hatred. He then co-founded the Justice and Development Party (AKP), which won a landslide in the 2002 election. As prime minister from 2003 to 2014, he oversaw economic recovery after the 2001 crisis, the start of EU membership negotiations, and a reduction in military influence on politics. In 2014 he became Turkey's first directly elected president. His presidency has been described as marked by democratic backsliding and a shift toward [[Authoritarianism|authoritarianism]], and his economic policies have been linked to high inflation and a depreciating lira. In 2022 he temporarily blocked [[Finland]] and [[Sweden]] from joining [[NATO]] and brokered a grain deal between [[Russia]] and [[Ukraine]].

State capital of [[Pernambuco]], on the northeastern Atlantic coast of [[Brazil]] (metro pop., 2022: 3,726,974). Founded in 1537 as the main harbor of the [[Sugarcane|sugar cane]]-producing Captaincy of Pernambuco, it was called Mauritsstad when it served as capital of the Dutch colony of New Holland in the 17th century. Its name alludes to the stone reefs offshore. Recife is the largest urban area in Brazil's North and Northeast regions. Its rivers, small islands, and more than 50 bridges give it a maritime character that has earned it the nickname "[[Venice]] of Brazil." The metropolitan region is the main industrial zone of Pernambuco, and private investment has made Recife Brazil's second largest medical hub, after [[São Paulo]]. The historic center of Olinda, 7 km north of the city, became a [[UNESCO|UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Site|World Heritage Site]] in 1982. Recife was a host city of the [[FIFA World Cup|2014 FIFA World Cup]].

Series of military campaigns by northern Iberian [[Christians|Christian]] states against Muslim-ruled [[Al-Andalus|al-Andalus]], which had been part of the [[Visigothic Kingdom]] before the Muslim conquest of 711. The campaigns are traditionally dated from the Battle of Covadonga (c. 718 or 722), when the army of the Kingdom of Asturias won the first Christian victory over the [[Umayyad Caliphate]]. After the Umayyad state of Córdoba broke into petty successor states called taifas in the early 11th century, the northern kingdoms advanced, and major Muslim centers fell in the 13th century, including [[Seville]] in 1248. The Catholic Monarchs took [[Granada]] in January 1492, ending Muslim rule on the peninsula. Under the Alhambra Decree of July 30, 1492, the Jewish communities of Castile and Aragon, some 200,000 people, were forcibly expelled. The term was not used by medieval writers, and it was associated with [[Nationalism|Spanish nationalism]] in the 19th century; historians have debated its meaning.

Period of United States history (1865–1877) after the [[American Civil War]], dominated by ending [[Slavery|slavery]] and reintegrating the former Confederate states. Three amendments granted freed slaves citizenship and equal civil rights, but Southern states used poll taxes and literacy tests to discourage Black voting. After [[Abraham Lincoln]] was assassinated in 1865, [[Andrew Johnson]] pardoned Confederate leaders, and Radical Republicans later enacted Reconstruction Acts over his vetoes. Violent groups, including the [[Ku Klux Klan]], terrorized Republicans. The Compromise of 1877 gave the disputed 1876 election to [[Rutherford B. Hayes]] in exchange for removing federal troops from the South, which historians generally mark as the end of Reconstruction. Critics cite its failure to prevent violence and corruption, while its defenders credit it with restoring the Union and establishing constitutional guarantees of equal protection.

Family of woodwind [[Musical instrument|instruments]] and the most prominent duct flute in the Western classical tradition. Recorders have a thumb hole and seven finger holes, and are made in soprano, alto, tenor, and bass sizes. Traditionally made of wood or ivory, modern professional instruments are often boxwood, while student instruments are commonly molded plastic. The recorder is first documented in Europe in the Middle Ages and was popular in the Renaissance and Baroque periods, but was little used in the Classical and [[Romantic music|Romantic]] periods. It was revived in the 20th century by the historically informed performance movement and became a popular educational instrument. Composers who wrote for it include Monteverdi, Purcell, [[George Frideric Handel|Handel]], and [[Johann Sebastian Bach|Bach]]. Its clear, sweet sound has historically been associated with birds and shepherds. Its English name, used since the 14th century, has no equivalent in Middle French.

Activity of [[Leisure|leisure]] done for enjoyment, amusement, or pleasure, often regarded as "fun." The need for recreation is an essential element of human biology and psychology. The English word, first used in the late 14th century, derives from [[Latin]] *re* ("again") and *creare* ("to create"). Leisure, the time free from physical and social needs, is a prerequisite of recreation, and it is a human right under the [[Universal Declaration of Human Rights]]. Recreation is difficult to separate from [[Play (activity)|play]], which is usually the term for children's activity, and from work, since playing an instrument may be a profession for one musician and a recreation for another. Recreation has health benefits, and therapeutic recreation specialists work in rehabilitation, psychiatric care, and the care of the elderly. Recreational physical activity helps reduce obesity and the risk of osteoporosis and some cancers.

Use of psychoactive drugs to induce an altered state of [[Consciousness|consciousness]], usually for pleasure or another casual purpose. Recreational drugs are commonly divided into depressants, which slow the central nervous system; stimulants, which speed it up; and hallucinogens, which induce perceptual distortions. Common examples include [[Caffeine|caffeine]] in coffee, tea, and chocolate, [[Alcohol (drug)|alcohol]] in beer and wine, and [[Nicotine|nicotine]] in tobacco. Substances controlled by law vary by country but often include [[Cannabis (drug)|cannabis]], cocaine, opioids, and MDMA. As of 2015, about 5% of people aged 15 to 65 (158 million to 351 million) had used controlled drugs at least once. Drug use is generally tolerated socially, though addiction is stigmatized. No single cause has been identified; experts apply a biopsychosocial model in which genetics, peer pressure, availability, and other factors interact. Since the early 2000s the [[European Union]] has pursued drug policies to prevent use and to counter [[Organized crime|organized crime]] and the illegal drug trade.

Process in which a definition or procedure depends on a simpler or earlier version of itself. Recursion ranges from [[Linguistics|linguistics]] to [[Logic|logic]], but it is most common in [[Mathematics|mathematics]] and [[Computer science|computer science]], where a function is applied within its own definition. A recursive definition has a base case and a recursive step that reduces all cases toward it. The [[Fibonacci sequence]], with F(0) = 0, F(1) = 1, and F(n) = F(n − 1) + F(n − 2) for n > 1, is a classic example. The Peano axioms define the [[Natural number|natural numbers]] recursively. A recursive procedure must skip the self-reference in some cases, or it would loop endlessly.

Process of converting [[Waste|waste]] materials into new materials and objects, often including the recovery of energy. As the third step of the reduce, reuse, and recycle waste hierarchy, recycling saves raw materials, lowers [[Greenhouse gas|greenhouse gas]] emissions, and avoids [[Air pollution|air pollution]] from incineration and [[Water pollution|water pollution]] from landfilling. Recyclable materials include glass, paper, cardboard, metal, plastic, [[Tire|tires]], textiles, batteries, and electronics, and composting food waste is also recycling. Metal cans can be remanufactured repeatedly without losing purity, while many other materials are turned into different products. Components of value or hazard, such as lead from car batteries, gold from [[Printed circuit board|printed circuit boards]], and mercury from thermometers, are salvaged from complex products. Paper recycling was first recorded in 1031, when Japanese shops sold repulped paper. Plastic recycling rates are low, around 9% globally, and critics argue that many programs are not economically viable without subsidies.

[[West Germany|West German]] far-left militant group, active from 1970 to 1998. Also called the Baader–Meinhof Group, it described itself as a communist and anti-imperialist urban guerrilla group. Early leaders included Andreas Baader, Ulrike Meinhof, and Gudrun Ensslin. Over three decades it carried out bombings, assassinations, kidnappings, and bank robberies. It is held responsible for 34 deaths, including the industrialist Hanns Martin Schleyer. Its activities peaked in 1977 during a national crisis known as the "German Autumn." Some ex-members later received support from the Stasi and other [[Eastern Bloc]] security services. In 1998 a letter faxed to [[Reuters]] declared that the group had dissolved.

Army and air force of the Russian Soviet Republic and, from 1922, the [[Soviet Union]]. Founded in January 1918 to fight the White Army in the [[Russian Civil War]], it was renamed the Soviet Army in 1946. Its performance was poor in the [[Winter War]] and early in [[Operation Barbarossa]], but it became highly effective. On the [[Eastern Front (World War II)|Eastern Front]] of [[World War II]] it fought the largest and deadliest land war in history and captured [[Berlin]]. Official Red Army losses in the war totaled 8,668,300, though other estimates reach almost 11 million. Red Army personnel also committed war crimes against civilians and prisoners of war.

Brand of energy drinks created and owned by the Austrian company Red Bull GmbH. It derives from the Thai drink Krating Daeng, which Austrian entrepreneur Dietrich Mateschitz encountered in Thailand in 1982, after finding it helped cure his jet lag. Mateschitz and Thai businessman Chaleo Yoovidhya founded the company in 1984, and the carbonated drink launched in Austria in 1987. Rather than conventional advertising, the brand built its image through [[Extreme sport|extreme sport]] events. It had a 13% share of the global energy drink market in 2023 and was the third most valuable soft drink brand in 2021, behind [[Coca-Cola]] and [[Pepsi]].

[[Mughal Empire|Mughal]] fort in Old Delhi, India, built as the main residence of the emperors. [[Shah Jahan]] commissioned it after moving the Mughal capital from [[Agra]] to Delhi. Its design is attributed to Ustad Ahmad Lahori, the architect of the [[Taj Mahal]]. Red sandstone walls enclose white marble palaces, and the fort combines Persian and Indian architectural styles. Completed in 1648, it was plundered by Nadir Shah in 1739, who seized its treasures, including the Peacock Throne. After the [[Indian Rebellion of 1857]], the British demolished many marble structures, although the defensive walls remained largely intact. On August 15, 1947, [[Jawaharlal Nehru]] raised the Indian flag above the Lahori Gate, and Indian prime ministers have done so each Independence Day since, delivering a broadcast address from its ramparts. The Red Fort Complex became a [[UNESCO|UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Site|World Heritage Site]] in 2007.

American rock band formed in Los Angeles in 1982, led by vocalist Anthony Kiedis and bassist Flea. Its music blends [[Alternative rock|alternative rock]], [[Funk|funk]], [[Punk rock|punk rock]], and [[Hip-hop|hip-hop]]. The album *Blood Sugar Sex Magik* (1991) brought the band major commercial success, and *Californication* (1999) became its biggest seller, with 16 million copies. The band holds the record for most number-one singles on the Alternative Songs charts, with 15. It was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2012 and received a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]] in 2022.

Inlet of the [[Indian Ocean]] between the [[Arabian Peninsula]] and [[Africa]]. It is about 2,250 km long and 355 km across at its widest point, with an area of roughly 438,000 sq km and an average depth of 490 m. Approximately 40% of its area is less than 100 m deep, and its shallow shelves support more than 1,000 invertebrate species and 200 types of coral. It is the world's northernmost tropical sea. Its southern connection to the ocean runs through the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait, and in the north it leads to the [[Suez Canal]] by way of the Gulf of Suez. The English name translates the [[Ancient Greek]] *Erythrà Thálassa*. The Biblical Hebrew name *Yam Suph* alludes to the parting of the sea for the [[Israelites]]. [[Ancient Egypt|Ancient Egyptians]] explored it around 2500 BCE in search of trade routes to Punt. Shipping through the sea fell substantially after late 2023 because of Houthi attacks.

Phylum of mostly marine [[Algae|algae]], among the oldest and largest groups of eukaryotic algae, with over 7,000 recognized species. Red algae lack flagella and centrioles, and their red color comes from phycobiliproteins, although many species appear green, brown, or nearly black. Unlike [[Green algae|green algae]], they store sugars as floridean starch outside the [[Chloroplast|chloroplasts]]. Most species reproduce sexually, through an [[Alternation of generations|alternation of generations]]. Coralline species secrete [[Calcium carbonate|calcium carbonate]] and help build [[Coral reef|coral reefs]]. Dulse (*Palmaria palmata*) and laver, or nori (*Porphyra* species), are traditional foods in European and Asian cuisines. Red algae are also used to make agar and carrageenans, which serve as food additives.

Most common type of blood cell, which delivers [[Oxygen|oxygen]] to the body's tissues as it passes through the capillaries. Red blood cells, also called erythrocytes, are rich in [[Hemoglobin|hemoglobin]], an iron-containing protein that binds oxygen and gives blood its red color. Each human red blood cell contains about 270 million hemoglobin molecules. Mature human red blood cells are flexible biconcave disks without a [[Cell nucleus|nucleus]] or organelles, which leaves more space for hemoglobin. Adults produce about 2.4 million new cells per second in the bone marrow. Cells circulate for about 100–120 days before macrophages recycle their components. Red blood cells make up roughly 40% to 45% of blood volume. Donated red cells are stored for [[Blood transfusion|transfusion]], and pulse oximetry uses the color change of hemoglobin to measure blood oxygen saturation.

Species of large [[Deer|deer]] (*Cervus elaphus*) native to most of [[Europe]], the Caucasus, Anatolia, Iran, and parts of western Asia. A male is called a stag or hart and a female a hind. Stags typically weigh 160 to 240 kg, and the red deer is the fourth-largest extant deer species. It is a [[Ruminant|ruminant]] with a four-chambered stomach. It is the only living deer species to inhabit Africa, where it lives in the [[Atlas Mountains|Atlas Mountains]]. Introduced populations live in [[Australia]], [[New Zealand]], and the [[United States]]. Although it was once rare in parts of Europe, it was never close to extinction, and reintroduction has increased populations in the United Kingdom and Portugal. Genetic evidence suggests the red deer is a species group, though the number of species remains disputed.

Smallest, coolest, and least luminous kind of [[Main sequence|main-sequence]] [[Star|star]]. Red dwarfs are the most common fusing stars in the [[Milky Way]], perhaps three-quarters of them according to some estimates. Their low luminosity means none is visible to the naked eye. [[Proxima Centauri]], the nearest star to the [[Sun]], is a red dwarf, as are fifty of the sixty nearest stars. Stars below 0.35 M☉ are fully convective, which remixes [[Helium|helium]] and lets a low-mass red dwarf keep a steady luminosity for trillions of years. The term has no strict definition; one of its earliest uses, in 1915, contrasted red dwarfs with hotter blue dwarfs.

Subspecies of pond slider [[Turtle|turtle]] (*Trachemys scripta elegans*) native to the southern United States and northern Mexico. It is named for the red stripe behind each eye and is popular as a pet worldwide. It is the most commonly traded chelonian and is included on the list of the world's 100 most [[Invasive species|invasive species]]. Released pets have established populations in [[Europe]] and [[Australia]], where they outcompete native species. Adults are typically 15 to 20 cm long, and females are usually larger than males. They typically live 20 to 30 years, sometimes more than 40, and live longer in captivity. Juveniles eat invertebrates, fish, and amphibians, while adults eat more plants. Females lay several clutches of 2–30 [[Egg|eggs]] a year. The species was formerly known as Troost's turtle, after herpetologist Gerard Troost.
